cards.originalFull:
To test dynamics sensitivity, $\Delta(\mathrm{GT} - \mathrm{Flat\,64})$ asks whether a metric can distinguish expressive resynthesis from a flat one. Among the similarity metrics, Pearson $r$ produces the larger separation on both BSSL ($+0.118$) and BSTL ($+0.263$). Cosine similarity also orders GT above flat, but it severely compresses the margin ($+0.052$ on BSSL and $+0.047$ on BSTL), proving \emph{insensitive} to fine dynamics differences.

To evaluate renderer robustness, $\Delta\lvert\mathrm{Sal.} - \mathrm{YDP}\rvert$ asks whether a metric is stable when the rendering SoundFont is swapped while the underlying note velocities are kept the same. Here, MAE proves \emph{over-sensitive} to absolute gain: it drifts by $0.193$ on BSSL and $1.723$ on BSTL, substantially more than the corresponding drift on $r$ ($0.034$ and $0.011$). On real recordings, this drift would conflate dynamics differences with renderer choice and make the evaluation unreliable.

Pearson $r$ on BSSL/BSTL therefore provides the right trade-off for this chapter. Cosine similarity and MAE fail on sensitivity and robustness, respectively, and are kept only as diagnostic alternatives. This is also the reason the main results table reports $r_{\mathrm{BSSL}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{BSTL}}$ as the headline metrics for label-free guitar evaluation.

options.label: v5 · 推荐短稿
options.fullText:
Both similarity metrics score GT above flat velocity in this diagnostic. Their numerical GT--flat gaps do not by themselves establish which metric is more sensitive to dynamics.

Changing from Salamander to YDP while retaining the GT notes and velocities changes MAE by $0.193$ on BSSL and $1.723$ on BSTL; the corresponding changes in Pearson $r$ are $0.034$ and $0.011$. This tests the effect of the renderer change as a whole, rather than absolute gain alone. Pearson $r$ is used here to compare loudness-contour agreement while reducing dependence on absolute level.

We therefore use Pearson $r$ on BSSL/BSTL as the main measure of rendered loudness-contour agreement for label-free guitar evaluation. In this piano diagnostic, it distinguishes GT from flat velocity under both tested SoundFonts. Cosine similarity and MAE are retained as complementary diagnostics.

cards.originalFull: This motivates the image-based view adopted in the present chapter. By treating symbolic MIDI as a sparse image and velocity as a colourisation target, the model can exploit local polyphonic structure more directly. U-Net and attention mechanisms are already successful in related music and audio tasks, but the present setting is distinct because it is purely symbolic and does not rely on acoustic input \cite{he2025filling,kim2024method}. This makes the chapter a natural starting point for the broader thesis.

options.fullText: We use piano rolls because the U-Net processes two-dimensional pitch--time neighbourhoods, including simultaneous notes. The input is binary and the output is a single-channel velocity roll, so colourisation is an analogy for adding dynamics to existing notes. A note-list representation would require a different model interface \cite{he2025filling,kim2024method}.

This representation supports the convolutional U-Net and window attention used here \cite{he2025filling,kim2024method}.

cards.reviewerComment: Section 3.2 and beyond considers the proposed work as “image-based”. Although there are some related figures with varying colours included in this chapter, I do not see any strong argument for using this term – the methodology does not treat dynamics as a colour channel or similar.
cards.authorResponse:
> Good question. The idea originally came from image-processing papers, especially the use of U-Net and window attention. We use “image-based” because both the input and output are two-dimensional pitch–time matrices, processed with two-dimensional convolutions.
>
> The input is a binary piano roll, and the output is a single-channel velocity roll. We do not predict RGB colours. “Colourisation” is an analogy for adding velocity values to the existing note structure, it's good for general audiance understand, but I agree that the wording needs clarification.
>
> I would say the “image-like” is more proper. I will make revision.

items.label: Justify Huber versus MAE without overstating what the actual author response established.
Local source-integrity repair found during independent audit, beyond v4. Do the table values establish insensitive cosine?
Does swapping a SoundFont isolate absolute gain?
Keep a positive reason for the chosen headline metric without claiming a validated universal metric ranking.
Avoid a background universal causal claim inconsistent with later conditional DDSP mismatch interpretation.
Define weakly expressive and weak supervision.
Would audio-to-MIDI-velocity also be a scenario, particularly Chapter 6?
Explain image-based/colourisation and piano roll versus note lists.
Is separate velocity refinement ecologically valid? Joint modelling may improve notes.
Why an explicit change-point head rather than beat/downbeat level predictions alone?
Do not assert modelling simplicity without evidence; author suggested efficiency but no cost comparison.
Distinguish co-authored paper methods from thesis synthesis.
Clarify which conclusions transfer to guitar, voice, bowed strings, winds.
Listening test with 11 experts supports objective results, not definitive perceptual validation.
